title: Sick, Betrayed, and Still Upheld
overview: A sick man who is mocked by enemies and betrayed by a close friend asks the LORD for mercy and healing, and trusts he will be kept safe.

parts.label: Kindness to the weak (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The psalm opens by saying the LORD looks after people who look after the poor and the weak, keeping them alive and safe from those who wish them harm. The picture in verse 3 is of a caring nurse who props up the patient and makes their sickbed comfortable.

parts.label: A plea for healing (v. 4)
parts.note: The speaker, traditionally David, asks for mercy and healing and admits he has done wrong. People then often linked illness with wrongdoing, so asking to be healed and asking to be forgiven went together.

parts.label: Visitors who want him dead (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: His enemies hope he dies and is forgotten, and some visit his sickbed only to collect gossip to spread. The Hebrew words for his illness in verse 8 are unclear, and scholars are unsure whether they mean a deadly disease or a wicked slander that has stuck to him.

parts.label: Betrayed by a friend (v. 9)
parts.note: Even a trusted friend who ate at his table has turned on him, a deep betrayal because sharing a meal meant a bond of loyalty. In the Gospel of John, Jesus quotes this verse about Judas, and Christians read the line in light of that betrayal.

parts.label: Raise me up (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: He asks the LORD to restore him so he can pay his enemies back, a frank wish that interpreters read either as personal payback or as a king's duty to bring wrongdoers to justice. He takes the fact that his enemies have not won as a sign that God is pleased with him and keeps him close.

parts.label: Closing praise (v. 13)
parts.note: This line praises the God of Israel for all time, past and future, and closes the first of the five collections that make up the book of Psalms. It was likely added to round off the whole collection, not just this psalm.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the psalm is mainly David's own prayer from his sickbed that Jesus later applied to himself, or a deliberate prediction of Jesus' betrayal by Judas.
think: When someone is at their weakest, what do you think shows who their real friends are?
